prompt: Ten independent metrics, none of which really moved, are each tested at 5%. What is the chance, in per cent to the nearest whole number, that at least one looks significant?
A secondary metric comes out significant while the primary does not. How should it be reported?

choices.text: As the test's main finding
choices.why: That swaps the primary metric after seeing the data.

choices.text: As a hypothesis for the next test
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Not at all, since secondary metrics must never appear in a report about a test
choices.why: They are reported as descriptions, just not as findings.

choices.text: As significant, if p is below 0.01
choices.why: A stricter cut for one hand-picked metric is still picking.

prompt: The calculation 1 − 0.95ᵏ assumes independent metrics. What happens with correlated ones, such as orders and revenue?

choices.text: Lower risk, same shape
choices.why: Right. Correlated metrics tend to cross together, so they add fewer independent chances.

choices.text: The risk disappears
choices.why: Correlation lowers it; it does not remove it.

choices.text: The risk doubles, since each correlated pair crosses the line together and counts twice
choices.why: Crossing together means fewer separate alarms, not more.

choices.text: The formula becomes exact
choices.why: It is exact only for independent metrics.

prompt: On mobile the new checkout lifted conversion 0.62 points with p = 0.006, among nine segments examined. panela.py gives every device the same effect. What is the mobile finding?

choices.text: A real difference between devices
choices.why: The data was built with none.

choices.text: Proof that lesson 7's hypothesis was right
choices.why: Fitting a story makes it more tempting, not more likely.

choices.text: A sample ratio mismatch on mobile
choices.why: The groups were balanced on device in lesson 9.

choices.text: Noise that crossed the line by chance among the nine slices examined
choices.why: Right. After Holm it is not significant.

prompt: Why is a segment result that confirms the team's belief especially dangerous?

choices.text: Confirming segments are always wrong
choices.why: They can be right; they deserve the same scrutiny.

choices.text: It inflates the sample
choices.why: Nothing about the sample changes.

choices.text: Nobody doubts it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Statistics forbids testing a hypothesis twice, so the second test can only repeat the first
choices.why: Testing it again in a new experiment is exactly the right move.

prompt: What is the honest next step after the mobile finding?

choices.text: Ship the change only on mobile
choices.why: On evidence that does not survive correction.

choices.text: A new test of it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Report it as the main result
choices.why: It was not the planned question.

choices.text: Drop the desktop visitors from the data and rerun the original test on mobile only
choices.why: That is the same slice under another name.

prompt: With nine comparisons and an overall 5% level, what threshold does Bonferroni set for each p-value? Answer to four decimal places.
Why prefer Holm to Bonferroni when software does the arithmetic?

choices.text: Same promise, more power
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Holm accepts some false findings
choices.why: That is the false discovery rate.

choices.text: Holm needs no p-values at all, because it works directly from the counts of each group
choices.why: It works on the sorted p-values.

choices.text: Bonferroni is only for two comparisons
choices.why: It works for any number.

prompt: A team screens 500 products to choose which to test next. Which correction fits?

choices.text: None
choices.why: With 500 comparisons about 25 will cross by chance.

choices.text: Bonferroni
choices.why: So strict at 500 that it would miss almost everything real.

choices.text: Holm
choices.why: Same guarantee as Bonferroni, and nearly as strict at this scale.

choices.text: The false discovery rate
choices.why: Right. It controls the share of false findings, which suits a screening.

prompt: Which comparison needs no correction at all?

choices.text: The segment with the smallest p-value
choices.why: Picking the smallest is exactly the problem.

choices.text: Every guardrail, since guardrails are watched for harm and harm never needs to be corrected
choices.why: Many guardrails checked for harm still multiply chances of a false alarm.

choices.text: The primary metric chosen before the test
choices.why: Right. Choosing it in advance is the protection.

choices.text: A weekday breakdown
choices.why: Seven comparisons.

prompt: In the simulation, what share of A/A tests declared a winner when read every day, in per cent?
Why simulate A/A tests to study peeking?

choices.text: A/A tests have more visitors
choices.why: The size is the same.

choices.text: Any winner there is false
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: They are faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Real tests cannot be peeked at
choices.why: They can, and that is the problem.

prompt: During a test, when is it right to stop early?

choices.text: When a guardrail is clearly worse
choices.why: Right. Stop for harm, not for joy.

choices.text: When the primary metric crosses p < 0.05
choices.why: That is peeking.

choices.text: When the lift looks larger than the MDE
choices.why: Still deciding on the primary metric early.

choices.text: Every Friday, so that the weekend does not distort the result of the test
choices.why: Whole weeks exist to include the weekend.

prompt: How does a sequential test allow early looks without raising the false-alarm rate?

choices.text: It ignores the early data
choices.why: It uses it, with stricter thresholds.

choices.text: It uses a one-sided test
choices.why: Sidedness is a separate choice.

choices.text: It adds visitors to every look so that each look has as many as the full test would
choices.why: Visitors cannot be added; the thresholds change.

choices.text: It demands a much smaller p-value at each of the early looks, which are planned in advance
choices.why: Right. The 5% is spent across looks decided in advance.

prompt: Match each correction or practice to what it protects against.

pairs.right: a false alarm among a handful of segments
too many false findings in a large screening
stopping when noise crosses the line

prompt: Order the ways of reading the simulated A/A tests from the lowest to the highest false-alarm rate.
items: every day, stopping at the first crossing
